There are, I venture to say, many men in this country who gathered at the Liberal convention of 1919 and helped to formulate the platform-men who have not been trained in political acrobatics as the leader of the Opposition has and who find it impossible to follow the contortions of that gentleman in political matters. I cannot conceive and I cannot believe that the men who gathered at that convention from all parts of Canada and after careful deliberation, formulated, a platform, can continue to recognize as a true leader a gentleman who has saerified them-sacrificed his party, the platform of that party, and every pledge he made- on the altar of political expediency, at one time in one constituency supporting a candidate who repudiates most emphatically one part of his platform and on another occasion supporting another candidate who repudiates another part of his platform. It seems to me, Sir, that the leader of the

Opposition, in view of his record during the past year, is the last man who should ask the leader of the Government by what right he holds his present position.
The leader of the Opposition has accused the Government of being usupers. Usurpers indeed! Are we then to consider as usurpers the men who have consistently adhered to a policy which has been the recognized policy on tariff matters in this country for forty years? Are we to consider those men usurpers and to regard as bona fide a gentleman who for the sake of attaining to the position of leader of a party endorsed a platform in its entirety and broke almost every plank of that platform as soon as he assumed the office which he now holds? If any person, is entitled to be called a usurper of office it is the present leader of the Opposition.
That hon. gentleman has stated that in the election of 1917 there was only one issue before the country and that issue was the war. He laboured at some length by quotations from the speeches of hon. gentlemen on this side to show that that was the only issue in the election of 1917. I think he exerted himself needlessly in that regard. There was one issue in the election of 1917 and that issue was of such vast importance as to overshadow every other thought that might be in the mind of a man running for Parliament. I think, therefore, it is quite right to say that the issue, and practically the only one, in the last election was the war and the carrying of it on to a successful conclusion. There were strong reasons for doing what was done at that time; there were strong reasons why that should be the issue. In 1914 we obtained by voluntary enlistment some ninety-six thousand men in Canada. In 1915 we obtained one hundred and ten thousand. In 1916 we obtained one hundred and seventy-nine thousand. In 1917 we obtained only fifty-six thousand. No one will claim that the need for men was less in 1917 than it was in any of the preceding years-the need was greater.
In Great Britain the need was recognized by all classes of the population and by none more so than by the women. Sir, some two million eight hundred thousand women in that little island were engaged in what may properly be called war service. Two hundred and seventy thousand of them were engaged in agriculture, tilling the fields and .reaping the crops. Eight hundred and nineteen thousand were engaged in the metal trades; over seven hundred thousand were engaged in making munitions, and sixteen thousand five hundred were working in the shipyards. There was strong need if we were to maintain our national honour and be true to our pledge to back up the boys who had gone overseas, for the action that was taken in 1917, and good and sufficient cause why the war should be the main and practically the only issue.
During the years up to the election of 1917 the Government of this country was burdened with such responsibility as I venture to say never fell to the lot of any previous Government in Canada. Nevertheless they carried on. During those years the present leader of the Opposition was in a foreign country in close association with the greatest and most unscrupulous profiteering plutocrat on the face of the earth. When the election came on and the issue was whether Canada was true to the boys overseas or not-that in a word was what the issue amounted to-the present leader of the Opposition returned to Canada, became a candidate in the election, and did all he possibly could to prevent reinforcements from being sent overseas.
That was his attitude at that time, and no amount of declamation, no amount of bombast and no amount of vociferous vituperation on the part of the leader of the Opposition can hide that record. It is there, the people of this country know it- and when I say "the people of this country" I mean the people of all parties in this country. I am sure I am speaking what is right when I say that thousands of Liberals from one end of Canada to the other will never follow the hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition, and that they would regard it as a calamity if he ever came to occupy the position of Prime Minister.
My hon. friend from St. James (Mr. Rinfret) said it was striking how history repeats itself. Yes, there are some striking examples of that. Away back in 1867, when men were just as strong-willed as are the men of to-day, when they were just as partisan as are their descendants of the present day, there were men big enough and broad enough to lay aside their party differences of opinion and to unite for a great purpose. Fifty years later history repeated itself, and the descendants of those men, to the everlasting honour of Canada, were big enough and broad enough to lay aside party differences and unite for a great purpose-the purpose of keeping faith with the boys who went over-



seas. Everybody knows the attitude of the men who were elected in 1917 on that great issue, and everybody knows the attitude of the hon. the leader of the Opposition. No amount of eloquence on his part can cover up his attitude at that time, nor make the red-blooded people of Canada have confidence in him.
The hon. the leader of the Opposition says that this Parliament has no right to deal with the tariff issue. He asked the question: Will any one say that the tariff is an issue arising from the war? Well, I would say: Yes, most emphatically, beyond question the tariff is an issue arising from the war. Can any person question that we have changed international commercial relations to-day, and that those changed relations have been brought about and are directly due to the great conflict through which we have passed? Every country in the world has been forced to recognize the effect which that war has had upon international commercial relations, and every country is studying the problem now and taking steps to adjust its tariff to meet the changed conditions. Most certainly the tariff, as it has been forced upon us by the war, is a condition arising from the war. The hon. gentleman says that we should not deal with the tariff, that it should be dealt with only by a Parliament truly representative of the people. Well, he did not hold that view last year. What has brought about the change in his mind? In the debates of last session he thought it was all right for a tariff resolution to be brought down and debated. What makes the difference between now and this time last year with regard to this Parliament dealing with the tariff?
But let us take him at his word. The tariff is a very important matter. I could quote from a great many public men, including the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding), who for fifteen years held the office of Finance Minister and had much to do with tariff matters- I could quote him and many others to the effect that the tariff can not be tinkered with every few months, but has to be dealt with periodically. While I quite appreciate the importance of dealing with the tariff, my own opinion is that this Parliament would make a mistake if it dealt drastically with it at this session. It may be advisable to make certain changes and alterations, but I do not think the present time opportune to make any very general changes, especially in view of the fact that our principal trade is with our neighbour

to the south and with Great Britain. A new party has been elected to office in the United States, a party which gave very definite and positive pledges in regard to tariff revision, and it seems to me that it would be the part of wisdom for this Parliament to defer a general revision of the trtiff until our neighbours to the south have given some indication, as they are bound to give, in redemption of their recent election pledges. We are more dependent upon the United States so far as this matter is concerned than they are upon us.
But appreciating the importance, Mr. Speaker, of dealing with the tariff, if it is advisable that it should only be dealt with by a Parliament truly representative of the people, then it seems to me that the leader of the Opposition in that very circumstance has adva.nced a good reason why there should not be a dissolution. This Parliament cannot be taken as truly representative of the people from the standpoint of representation by population; that can only be remedied after the census is taken. A few months from now that census will be taken, and after a redistribution we will have a Parliament truly representative of the peoeple, assuming, of course, that the redistribution will take into consideration the changes in population in the various provinces and in the various centres. No one can reasonably argue that an hon. gentleman representing a constituency of fifteen or twenty thousand people should have a say which would be as strong as that of three representatives from other parts. Yet it is true that until redistribution is effected we shall have some members representing a population of 70,000 or 80,000, while others, as in the case of the hon. gentleman from Brome (Mr. McMaster) represent a population of 13,000 or 14,000. So far as the matter affects the question of a parliament truly representative of the people dealing with the tariff, I do not think it needs any argument. '
The member for St. James stated that fourteen members had been elected to this side in 1917 by the soldier vote; at least, that is the way I understood him. The statement of the hon. member is absolutely incorrect. I have before me a summary of the general election returns for 1917. All but four of the 82 members who were elected to this House from Ontario were elected by the civil vote, without regard to the soldier vote at all. Of the four, three were Conservative-Unionists and one

was a Liberal-Unionist. It is not unreasonable to suppose that the member elected for any constituency would have obtained at least as large a proportion of the votes of the soldiers overseas as he would of the votes of the soldiers who cast their ballots at home. If you allowed the member for Essex South only the same percentage of overseas votes as he received of the home soldier vote and gave the other votes to his opponent, he would still have a comfortable majority. That narrows it down to only three seats in Ontario which could possibly have been affected by any manipulation of the soldier vote, and there has been no charge that the slightest attempt was made to manipulate the soldier vote in Ontario.
Let us consider the province of Quebec. Out of sixty-five seats it is true that on that occasion only three supporters of the Government were elected. The hon. Minister of Marine had 1,446 of a majority of the civil vote, and 1,957 of a majority of the soldier vote, so that he could have made a present of 1,000 votes to his opponent and still have a majority of some 1,400. The member for St. Antoine had a majority of 1,583 of the civil vote; he could have given his opponent 1,000 soldier votes and still have had a majority of 1,100. In the case of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), he had a majority of 2,099 of the civil vote, and could have given his opponent 1,000 of his soldier votes and still have had a majority of 1,930. Surely the members of the Opposition who were elected by acclamation in 1917 have no grievance so far as any alleged manipulation of votes is concerned. I do not think that many hon. gentlemen on the other side were very deeply concerned or very much affected by the soldier vote. The member for Yamas-ka got eight soldier votes, all told. The member for St. Denis got 199 and one of his opponents got five. The member for Kamouraska received 11 soldier votes and his opponent 4. The member for Joliette received none and his opponent 3. So that for some reason the soldier vote did not seem to cut much ice down there; there did not seem to be many soldier votes in the province of Quebec.
I could give the details of the votes in all the other provinces, but I will sum it up in this statement which I have made before in the House, and which I am prepared to prove; that not one hon. member sitting in this House owes his majority to any manipulation of the soldier vote. Every hon. gentleman elected to this House in
1917 would have been elected if you accorded to him the same percentage of the overseas vote as he received of the home soldier vote and gave the balance to his opponent. I have the figures which will prove my statement to the hilt. Therefore, the remarks of the hon. member for St. James this afternoon in this connectibn are not borne out by the facts. The hon. member for St. James referred to several things in connection with which he considered the Government delinquent. But he did not go into details; he simply made a general, blanket statement, asserting that the Government's railway policy was wrong, that there had been extravagance, and so on.
I can only assume that the reason why the hon. member did not attempt to back up his general statement with details was because he had no details with which to back them up-that is the only conclusion that I can come to.
But I should like to ask the hon. gentleman:	If the Government was guilty of
any of the sins or delinquencies which he charges them with, why did his leader move an amendment in such bald and naked terms? Why did his leader not move an amendment condemning the Government for some act that the Government had performed or some delinquincies on the part of the Government? It is strange that in all these by-elections, in all the , speeches made from one end of the country to the other by the leader of the Opposition and those that supported him, they have unconsciously paid a tribute to the Government that, they say, should resign office because, while the Government has had a lot of work to do and has had to deal with millions and hundreds of millions of dollars, particularly during these years of the war, the Opposition, in all their speeches, have made no specific charges against the Government in regard to their conduct of public business. They have not said: This Government should resign office because, during the years since 1917, it has failed to redeem its pledges to the people; it has failed to do properly the work which fell! upon it to do. The only reason advanced by the leader of the Opposition is in effect: You have performed the work that you were supposed to perform and you have done it well, so well indeed that I am not finding any fault with it; but we want you to step down and out, because we want a chance to get in. Talk about holding on to office! There never was, I suppose, an hon. gentleman who took any part in the

political life of this country who has manifested such a crazy eagerness and at the same time an entire unfitness for office as the leader of the Opposition.
By-elections! West Peterborough, the one to which my hon. friends like to refer! Well, the by-election in West Peterborough resulted as it did. West Peterborough at least elected a man who repudiated the platform of the leader of the Opposition and was assisted in the election by that leader himself. That is the situation so fas as West Peterborough is concerned. But the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret) quotes'some remarks made by the former member for Peterborough West, Mr. Burnham, in which he expresses his opinion as to what should be done, and says that Parliament should dissolve, that there should be a general election. Does the leader of the Opposition hold that view? Apparently, yes. Why does not the leader of the Opposition show by acts that he holds that view? Why is it that he permits one of his principal lieutenants to hold two seats in this House? Why does he not prevail upon him to resign one of those seats and bring that question up as a great issue? The reason why, it seems to me, is about the same as the reason why his amendment is so naked and bald as it is. We are told by the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Rouville (Mr. Gauthier) that one of the constituencies to which I refer is a constituency which would be disposed to favour free trade and that the other constituency is just as strongly disposed towards protection. The leader of the Opposition, who is so extremely courageous in regard to wanting a general election, is afraid to open the constituency which favours free trade for fear that he would have to appear on the platform and endorse, rather more openly than he cares to do down in this part of the country, the doctrine of free trade. He is equally afraid to have the other constituency opened for fear that he would be obliged, more openly than he cares to do, to advocate a policy of protection and thus lose some of the support which he hopes to get in the West, and which he will never get. That is one of the reasons why, I think, he does not allow one of those constituencies to have representation in this House, why he does not test out his view by having the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux), who represents Gaspe and Maisonneuve, resign one of those seats and give an opportunity for an election. The leader of the Opposition has not 
shown any very strong disposition for an election in the past. It is true he has talked of elections, but when the elections were on in St. John and Colchester, the hon. gentleman, who was talking of elections and saying: "Oh, yes, we want to go to the country; we want to test public opinion, did not put up a man in Colchester and test public opinion. He took good care not to go down there; he went three thousand miles away. That is characteristic of the hon gentleman; he has done most of his fighting at a distance of about three thousand miles.
I could quote from remarks .made, in times past, by many hon. gentlemen opposite, which, I think, would very strongly support this Government in the attitude it has taken, and support the members on this side in taking the course which they are taking. We have on this side men who, it is true, were elected as Liberal Unionists, others who were elected as Conservative Unionists, men who previously to 1917 followed one or other of the old political parties. On the other side of the House we have some hon. gentlemen saying that certain gentlemen on this side are untrue to Liberal principles in staying on this side of the House. I could quote from the utterances of a number of very prominent men to show that any Liberals who were elected in 1917 to sit on this side of the House are more consistent in sitting here and supporting this Government than they would be if they went across and sat behind the leader of the Opposition. What was the attitude of the Liberal party as regards the tariff for the fifteen years it was in power? Was its attitude for the fifteen years it was led by the late Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier in keeping with the platform of the Liberal party as laid down in August, 1919? Not by any means. Take for instance, the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier in regard to the industries of the country. I am quoting now from a speech which was sent broadcast throughout the country, a speech delivered by that right hon. gentleman on the 7th March, 1911. He says:
I pass to a more important objection-
He was speaking of reciprocity.
-really the only objection of any consequence that I know of. That objection is that this agreement will imperil our industries. How will it imperil our industries ? This agreement is concerned chiefly with natural products. There are no manufactured products dealt with in it except agricultural implements.

He might have gone on and said there was no very serious reduction made on agricultural implements. It is true that the attitude of the Liberal party of that day, led by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, was in favour of taking the duties off foodstuffs, but so far as manufactured articles were concerned he made it very clear indeed that his attitude and the attitude of his party was not to interfere with the industries of this country. Therefore, I say that hon. gentlemen who are sitting on this side of the House are more consistent in their attitude on the trade policy of this country, which has been followed by all Governments for the last forty years, than are hon. gentlemen who sit on the other side of the House, and who laid down a platform-and that is the only guide we have as to their views-which they say themselves it is not advisable to attempt to carry out. Take, for instance, the statement of the hon. member for Shelbourne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) in the House last session. Discussing the tariff, he said:
I do not thitak myself, as things are going now, that we can look to that party for a sound tariff policy.
He was speaking of the Farmers' party. I entirely agree with him. I do not think we can. He went on:
What then? I do not even think we can expect to g-et a sound and safe tariff policy by a too rigid adherence to every line and every letter of the Liberal Tariff platform. I think myself that we will find that we are all prone in framing platforms to put things perhaps a little more strongly than is wise, and we all find when we come to the responsibly of office that we may have to modify our views.
What faith, Mr. Speaker, can you place in a party which has for one of its principal men a man who can make a statement like that?. The hon. member for Shelbourne and Queen's took part recently in the election in Peterborough, and of course he was told by the Liberal candidate there that it would not do to talk free trade in Peterborough, but, on the contrary, an assurance must be given to the people of that industrial centre that their industries would not be imperilled. What was the attitude of the hon. gentleman? Did he get up and quote to them from the platform of the Liberal party framed at the convention in Ottawa in August, 1919? No, Mr. Speaker, on the contrary he gets up and says:	Why be alarmed, you Liberals,
for your industries? Did we not make promises previous to 1896? Did we not say from one end of Canada to the other that
if we only had an opportunity we would destroy protection root and branch, obliterate it entirely,-that was our statement in 1896, but gentlemen, did we do it?-for fifteen years we went back on the pledges and promises we had made previous to 1896; for fifteen years we proved false to the pledges which we had given throughout this country in the preceding eighteen years, so, surely, you men of Peterborough need no further guarantee that we can be false to our pledges again.	,
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at 8 o'clock.

Mr Speaker, I had just about concluded my remarks before recess when you called it 6 o'clock. I have very few words to add to what I have already said, and I shall therefore occupy only a very few minutes more. I was about to call attention to a remark by the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret), who referred rather slightingly to certain members on this side of the House as weak-kneed reformers, and I believe that in connection with that remark he quoted some statement made some years ago by the late Hon. Edward Blake. Well, I presume there were people, tyros in politics like the hon. member, who years ago called Edward Blake names when he saw fit to dissociate himself from his leader on a great matter of public policy. I think, therefore, hon. members on this side may pass very lightly the derogatory remarks made by the hon. member for St. James in his speech.
Now, I want to put this question in all seriousness to the members of this House: Suppose this amendment should carry, what then? Let me give the opinion of the leader of the Opposition on that point. Speaking in the Peterborough election, as reported in the press, the hon. gentleman said that if this Government did as he claimed it should do and resigned, the constitutional procedure would be for His Excellency the Governor General to call upon the leader of the Opposition to form a Government and that the leader of the Opposition-of course, there is no doubt about this-would immediately accede to the request. That would not mean a general election; it would mean that the Cabinet ministers selected by the hon. gentleman would have to go to the country for election. So that in the event of this amendment carrying, the constitutional procedure would be that the hon. gentleman, on the advice of His Ex-
, 134

cellency, would endeavour to form a Government to carry on for the rest of the life of this Parliament, another year and a half or two years. On what mandate would he carry on? Is there any doubt that this is the course he would take? He has intimated that he would not proceed with a 'general tariff revision until he had put his house in order, and perhaps it would be several years before the question would be submitted to the people in regard to the tariff. The whole attitude of the hon. gentleman, borne out by his own speeches, goes to show that he is not, and has not been, actuated by high motives and lofty principles in making the demand he has made upon the Government to resign, but that he has been impelled solely by the desire to obtain office with the fruits thereof for himself. That is the situation.

I am sure the hon. member will allow me to make a statement in correction. He is purporting to quote a speech I made at Peterborough. If he will look at that speech he will discover that it is exactly the opposite of what he has said. What I stated in Peterborough was that if the present Government were defeated on a want of confidence vote, and the leader of the Opposition were called upon to form a Government, the Government so formed would not proceed to deal with the tariff, but would dissolve Parliament and have a general election and that the issue on the tariff would be discussed at that election. Nothing would be done by this Parliament to deal with the tariff one way or the other. This is the opposite of what my hon. friend has said.

Well, I wonder just how much nearer the people would be to relief if the hon. gentleman had his way, than if this Parliament continued for the rest of its term. The hon. gentleman says he would go ahead and form his Government. That would take some time; the year 1921 would be well on the way. I venture to say that if this motion carried and the hon. gentleman were called upon to form a Government, he would take good care that he put his fences in order as well as he possibly could. I think I am absolutely safe in saying that he would carry on until after redistribution had taken place. If he were called upon to form a Government, some time must elapse before he could get under way and the census, or at least that part of it relating to population, would have been taken. Does he mean to say that he wouid disregard that and proceed on the present distribution of
fMr. Edwards.]
constituencies and go to the people? I should like to ask him that question.
Ask him now.

I have been reminded that while it is perfectly proper for an [DOT] hon. member to ask me a question it is not competent for me, under the rules of the House, to ask another member any questions.
, I do not intend to be called to order in that regard again. There is only one other thing to which I wish to refer. In the speech made by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) and also in that of the hon. member for St. James, we find very slighting references by both gentlemen to what they term a desire on the part of the Prime Minister (Hon. Mr. Meighen) to court the favour of the province of Quebec. They declare that the Prime Minister has endeavoured to get Cabinet representation from that province; that being eager to obtain increased representation he has made overtures to the province of Quebec in that direction. Well, suppose that were true; is there anything unworthy in the supposition?
The province of Quebec is the oldest, the largest, and certainly one of the most important, of the provinces of Confederation. I am sure every person realizes and regrets -no one to a greater degree than the Prime Minister himself-the fact that Quebec has not greater representation in the Cabinet than it has to-day. Is it unworthy on the part of the Prime Minister that he should like to see that province with proper representation? Is that something to provoke sneers from' hon. gentlemen opposite? It seems to me that the thinking men of the province of Quebec will view this matter in a different light from the way in which hon. gentlemen opposite regard it, if we are to judge from their remarks.
What does it disclose? We had some time ago, and from time to time we still have, little scraps in the Globe. The editorial utterances of that paper indicate the object and purpose of the whole propaganda. The Globe on the 4th August last said that the present Prime Minister had made a speech in this House bitter and stinging in its hostility and antagonism to the province of Quebec. The Prime Minister, speaking in the city of Sherbrooke, referred to this statement of the Toronto Globe and explicitly and most emphatically denied it, and he asked that paper to publish one single line or sentence

that he had ever uttered at any time indicating hostility or unfriendliness to Quebec.
Up to date the Globe has made no attempt to justify the lying assertion which its columns contained on the 4th August. It was and is a part of the plan of that paper to assist gentlemen like the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), the hon. member for St. James, and others, in carrying on a propaganda the purpose and object of which is to solidify the people of that Province against fhis Government by appeals to race prejudice. That is the whole purpose and object of these gentlemen, and that is what is behind the sneers which they pass across the floor of the House to the Prime Minister who in exhibiting friendliness for the province of Quebec to-day as Prime Minister is exhibiting a sentiment no different from that which he has manifested throughout his public life. It is a cheap kind of political propaganda, it is an unworthy propaganda to carry on, but it is the kind of propaganda which has been and is still being carried on by certain hon. gentlemen opposite. I am glad to know that there is at least one member from the province of Quebec, the hon. member for St. Hyaeinthe-Rouville (Mr. Gauthier) who has disassociated himself from such unworthy attacks as those indulged in by the member for Brome and the juvenile member for St. James.
I challenge the leader of the Opposition, or any of those sitting behind him, to quote one single sentence, one single line, one single thought expressed in words by the present Prime Minister of Canada at any time, in this House or out of it, which has indicated the slightest feeling of hostility or unfriendliness to the people of the province of Quebec. I do not wonder at the member for Brome giving utterance to such statements as those referred to, but the member for St. James is a young man and being a young man he should have one of the characteristics of youth-he should have courage and he should have the courage to tell the truth. And Mr. Speaker while the Globe took a course in regard to the Prime Minister which it could not justify and has never attempted to justify, the member for St. James this afternoon was careful not to make a specific charge of such a character against the Prime Minister or any member sitting on this side. In the speech that he had prepared for circulation in the province of Quebec he arranged his words for the express purpose of conveying a thought which
he had not the courage to give utterance to in this Chamber.
I, Mr. Speaker, have more confidence in the judgment and sense of fair play of the people of Quebec than have these hon. gentlemen who profess to speak for that province, and my confidence in their judgment and sense of fair play is such that I believe in the course of time they will ask the men who are making these charges and indulging in these unwarranted statements to back up their charges and assertions with facts, and back them up in a way that will leave no doubt as to their truth or falsity. Because you cannot fool the people all the time My hon. friends from Brome and St. James may think that they can make unfounded statements with impunity, statements which will be accepted by the people of Quebec, but the time will come when the people will demonstrate that they are fair minded, and that they are going to judge these questions on their merits and judge public men according to their undoubted record. On that issue, and judged in that manner, I have no doubt as to the result of the next election when it comes.
This Parliament was elected for a period of five years. It has carried on during the very trying years of the war and during the years which have succeeded the war- the years of reconstruction, perhaps even more trying than when the war was actually in progress. Because, Sir, while the war was on there was the cement of a common peril and a common danger to hold in check the making of reckless statements by certain hon. gentlemen opposite and some others throughout the country. But at the conclusion of the war unrest developed, as it always has developed after every great struggle, and the difficulties of the Government were accentuated. The problems which faced the Government, and the burden of responsibility which rested upon them, should have been such as to appeal to all patriotic Canadians to refrain from other than constructive criticism and to give a helping hand in the heavy task which confronted the Administration. As I said earlier in the day, one of the best tributes paid to the efficiency of this Government has unconsciously been paid to it by the leader of the Opposition, and those who toured with him, in the speeches they delivered in every province, because the burden of their cry in those speeches was not that there had been mal-administration or lack of efficiency by the Government or any of

the departments in handling public affairs. It was merely the clap-trap in regard to a mandate such as we have heard from that leader and from some of those who have attempted to echo his words.
Extravagance and bad handling of the finances of this country! What have they brought in support of such general statements? If you compare the financial situation of Canada on the 31st March, 1920, with its position on the 31st March, 1914, you will certainly find that the national debt has been largely increased; but if you look carefully into those finances, and the records of the Finance Department will bear me out, it will be found, Mr. Speaker, that taking into consideration some $246,000,000 of capital expenditure other than investments, in the period of time I have mentioned, the Government of Canada not only carried on under their heavy burdens and responsibilities, but out of the revenues of the Dominion they paid off obligations to the extent of over $640,000,000, nearly twice as much as our net debt the year before the war.
And, Mr. Speaker, they also make charges against this Government regarding its management of the finances of the country.
I ask those who make those charges to compare the financial position of the Dominion with that of other countries engaged in the war. They will find-and I make this statement believing it to be true-that the financial position of Canada is better than that of any other belligerent country, with the exception of the United States, and that the debt per capita at the conclusion of peace was less than that of any other country engaged in the war, with the exception of the United States.
Not only that, Sir, but during the war, while the Government practised the most rigid economy in regard to public expenditure, there was one class to which they gave special consideration. I refer to the agriculturists. I think the records will bear me out that during the years of the war and since, notwithstanding the financial obligations which were pressing upon us from all sides, federal assistance to agriculture was from three to four times as great as it was in the years previous to 1914. Add to that the fact, Sir, that our forests and mines and fisheries during the years I have mentioned have doubled their production, and that agriculture and manufacturing have trebled their output since 1914; and add to that the further fact that notwithstanding the generous contributions of the people to the various Victory 
Loans, amounting to about $2,000,000,000, on the 31st March, 1920, the savings deposits of our people were 87 per cent greater than they were on the>
31st March, 1914, or 7 per cent greater than those of the people of the United States for exactly the same period of time. These figures do not indicate that the country has been going to the dogs under the Administration which has held power during the years of the war and since. These figures do not warrant the talk, unsupported by anything in the shape of detailed information, of hon. gentlemen opposite. And it is no wonder that the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret) limited himself to a mere general blanket accusation against the Government.
These are the reasons, Mr. Speaker, why the hon. the leader of the Opposition and his followers are asking for the resignation of this Government; but the very reasons advanced by these hon. gentlemen are an unconscious tribute to its efficiency. If the hon. the leader of the Opposition could have brought charges against this Government or against any department of it of mismanagement of our national affairs, does any person think for one moment that he would not have included them in his amendment? But no; that was not the purpose and object of the hon. gentleman. On the contrary, he presents a mere naked, bald amendment. For what purpose? To prevent an amendment being moved which might possibly divide hon. gentlemen sitting on the other side of the House, and naturally that is something he did not want to do. I commend again to the hon. leader of the Opposition, as I did this afternoon, the frank stand taken by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) when a question was put to him last year. Any public man, if he has the courage of his convictions, should not be afraid to answer a straight question candidly and say where he stands on the tariff.
But the hon. the leader of the Opposition is afraid to move an amendment to the Address in reference to the tariff, although an invitation to do so is contained in the Speech from the Throne. He is afraid to move an amendment embodying in distinctive and definite form a statement in regard to the tariff for fear he would find hon. gentlemen sitting across on my extreme right not exactly agreeing with such an amendment; he is afraid to move an amendment containing some of the views which he and the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) expressed in Peterborough in order to pull

the wool over the eyes of the people in that constituency who are interested in their local industries; he is afraid to move an amendment along the line of his speeches in Peterborough for fear that he would not get the votes of the hon. gentlemen to my right on the other side; he is afraid to move one along the free trade lines which he advocated when he was out in the Prairie Provinces, telling the farmers that there is really no dilference between the Farmers' platform and his platform. He dare not come down to the province of Ontario or to the province of Quebec and make such statements. It would not do. ' He is in the position of either simply voting for the motion on the Address, or of moving this naked, bald amendment of his, because he dare not move anything more specific.
Well, I should like the people all over the Dominion to compare the wabbling, twisting, tortuous course of the leader of the Opposition with the straightforward attitude assumed by the leader of this Government, as exemplified in their speeches from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Why, the twistings and turnings and contortions of the hon. the leader of the Opposition on political matters would make a snake turn green with envy. Where does he stand? He stands nowhere; he is like Mahomet's coffin-suspended between Heaven and Hell, and fit for neither place.
Mr. EMMANUEL d'ANJOU (Rimouski) (Translation) :	Mr. Speaker, before en-
' tering upon the few remarks I am about to make touching the amendment submitted by the hon. the Leader of the Opposition, I wish to answer very briefly the hon. member from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards). I wish the hon. gentleman could understand me as well as I understood him. However, he was entitled to use his mother tongue and I shall avail myself of the same privilege.
The hon. member from Frontenac wonders how it is that the hon. Leader of the Opposition should claim the right of leading the Liberal party in this House, and throughout the whole country. The hon. member ought to know that in November, 1919, there was held in Ottawa a large convention attended by delegates from every section of Canada, to elect the leader of the Liberal party who was to succeed the late lamented Sir Wilfrid Laurier. That Liberal convention was evidently a democratic one.
Consequently the hon. Leader of the Opposition can say that he is really the leader
of the Canadian Liberal party and he has a perfect right to claim, before this House and before the country, that he holds in his hands the destinies of the Liberal party. Quite another thing was the choice of the present Prime Minister. He was not chosen by a great democratic convention of delegates from all parts of the country called for the purposes of choosing a leader; the hon. Prime Minister was chosen by his partisans in this House, and as the hon. members who sit at your right, Mr. Speaker, do not represent the public opinion of the whole country, he is therefore not the choice of the whole of Canada.
The hon. member for Frontenac says also that thousands of Liberals, not only from the province of Ontario, but from all the provinces of Canada, refuse to recognize the hon. Leader of the Opposition as the leader of the Liberal party. Well, he forgets the result of the election which has just taken place in Peterborough West. At any rate, if he be so confident, if he is so sure of his statement, let him advise the hon. Prime Minister to dissolve the House, and he will see that the hon. Leader of the Opposition has followers everywhere in Canada.
The hon. member for Frontenac claims that not one of the members who sit on your right, Mr. Speaker, owes his election to the soldiers' vote. He forgets the message which was sent, in Algonquin dialect or in gibberish, I don't know which, by the hon. Prime Minister of to-day, directing that the soldiers' votes be distributed a little everywhere in different Western constituencies. This was never denied, and moreover the hon. Prime Minister himself has claimed in this House that he was perfectly justified in this course and that the electoral law was broad enough to allow it.
In reference to the election in West Peterborough the hon. member for Frontenac said that the hon. leader of the Opposition had contradicted himself in that county. Well, Mr. Speaker, as you know, that election took place after the resignation of Mr. Burnham, given on the ground that he claimed to have been elected as a partisan of the Union Government and that this government was to cease to exist at the conclusion of the war. He showed a little more courage than his friends. True this brought on his defeat, but at any rate the electors of Peterborough had an opportunity of making their views known, not on the question of the tariff, not on the question of free trade or protection, but on the question whether the electors of Peter-

borough as well as those of the rest of Canada were asking the overthrow of this government. The four opposition candidates were asking for a vote of non-confidence in the present administration, and the answer was eloquent.
The hon. member for Frontenac is also one of those who have fallen in love with the province of Quebec. It will be something new for the whole country to learn that the hon. member for Frontenac is holding Quebec close to his heart-especially its population. Never since the hon. member has held a seat in this House has the province of Quebec had a more violent traducer. But the disciple is worthy of the master. He follows his leader, the present Prime Minister, who now tries to fawn upon the province of Quebec, after having been the instigator of all the insults, the cowardly outrages and accusations heaped against that province in 1917. This party, in anticipation of its defeat, is ready to fall on its knees in the hope of roping in the province of Quebec and maintaining itself in power. Of the genuflexions of these gentleman I want none, but it is a pleasure to me to see them in such posture. One thing, however, must not be forgotten. If the province of Quebec knows how to forgive, it also knows how not to forget, and when the time comes it will remember the campaign of slander and calumnies which has been carried on through the whole country, and the principal instigator of which was the present leader of the Government. It will be all very well for him to try and make love and offer kisses of dubious sincerity to the electors of the province of Quebec, they will remember that he has been the chief organizer of that campaign of slander and race hatred carried on in order to juggle away power in 1917.
The hon. member for Frontenac talks of the fair play of the province of Quebec. That was not the talk we heard in 1917. We were then a disloyal province, a band of slackers. To-day, the province of Quebec is the model province, the Mecca of Canada. It is the fount of good principles, the resort where one may breath liberty and peace.
For Quebec, now-we can say it with pride-holds one of the most enyiable positions in the Confederation, not only in respect of the liberty enjoyed by all its citizens, but also of the wise and progressive administration which directs its destinies.

Mr. Speaker, many members have occupied the floor since the beginning of the present debate. No one, however, has spoken in the French language, which is one of the two official languages of the country. In accordance with my custom I wished to pay my tribute to Her Majesty the French language, and I wanted to be the first one to do so. Since I have had the honour of occupying a seat in this House- an honour I owe to my good and faithful friends the electors of the county of Ri-mouski-I have always, at every session, protested against the refusal of the Government to recognize the rights of the French language in this parliament. Thus, at every session, with the exception of that of 1918, the mover and seconder of the Address in answer to the Speech from the Throne were English speaking members, completely ignorant of the French language and consequently incapable of making their speech in French. The Government has no valid reason to cloak their refusal for, as ,1 have often had the opportunity of stating, they have in the ranks of their followers a member who is very well qualified to move or second the Address in quite good French, I mean my hon. friend the member for Edmonton East (Mr. Mackie).
It may perhaps be said in certain quarters, that this is after all but a question of detail, and that I attach too much importance to the matter. What might be said does not much matter; I am conscious of doing my duty by protesting as I do at this moment and as I did in the past. The saying is always true that the best, the surest way of keeping a right secure is to exercise it. That is why, every time I have had occasion to take the floor in this House, I have always used my maternal tongue-the beautiful French language- for I always attached, as I still do the greatest importance to the survival in this country of our sweet parlance from France.

Hear, hear.
Mr. d'ANJOU: I saw with great pleasure that the mover of the Address in the Senate paid us the delicate compliment of using French in the first part of his remarks. This honourable gentleman is to be congratulated, and he may be assured of the gratitude of all the French Canadians of the Dominion. It is evident that he did not consult the members of the Government before taking this gracious course, as otherwise he would have been given the formal order not to pronounce a single French word.

The new Prime Minister-the chief of the new tri-colour party-has missed a fine occasion to prove his sincerity towards the province of Quebec, which he has wooed and so frequently complimented since the usurpation of his present office.
If the province of Quebec is now dear to his heart, why has he not recognized the rights of the majority of its inhabitants by calling upon some of his partisans to move or second the Address in French? He has not done so, because he is not sincere. Besides, nobody can believe in the sincerity of the chief of the political mountebanks who, in order to win the election of 1917, did not hesitate to defame the province of Quebec and besmirch everything that is French in Canada.
The right hon. Minister of Commerce, in the course of his address about the League of Nations, told us that the two official languages at the assembly of the League were French and English. He even added that French was the dominant language at the assembly. French is the diplomatic language, and those who plume themselves upon belonging to the superior race should be able to understand and speak that language if they really wish to show their superiority over all other races.
Again, I condemn with the utmost energy the refusal of the Government to do justice to the French element in this country, by denying to the French language the place of honour which it has a right to occupy in the deliberations of the Canadian parliament.
Now, Mr. Speaker, as most of the hon. members who have preceded me, I will not tarry over the discussion of the more or less important questions brought forward in the speech from the Throne. The main question at this moment is whether in truth the present Government have a mandate from the people for the administration of the affairs of the country.
In the magnificent and powerful speech delivered by the hon. leader of the Opposition he over abundantly proved that the present Government have usurped power and that they have consequently no authority to direct the destinies of Canada.
The Prime Minister answers the arguments of the hon. leader of the Opposition by saying that he will remain in power as long as he can command a majority in the House of Commons. His majority, however, is but one of some twenty votes, fifteen of which are of members who have no right to their seats in the House since their election was due to the soldiers' vote. Such, Mr. Speaker, is what the hon. Prime Minister calls commanding the confidence of the House of Commons and consequently of the country at large.	.
At any rate, either this Government is the heir of the Union Government formed in 1917 for the duration of the war, or it is a government with a new head. In either case they hold no mandate from the people to govern the country.	_
It must not be forgotten that in 1917 this Government was constituted for one object only:	the carrying on and the ending of
the war. On all the hustings of the land, it was declared that this coalition was to end with the war. As you know, the war has long since come to its end, but nevertheless these gentlemen contend that they have the right to continue to direct the affairs of the country, because, as they say, they have behind them the majority of the House. They may truly have a majority, but, as I said a moment ago, what sort of a majority? A majority composed of members elected through the manipulation of the soldiers' vote, thanks to the iniquitous Wartime Elections Act, thanks to the disfranchisement of loyal Canadian citizens. And it is with a majority thus obtained that the Government mean to carry on the affairs of the country.	*
As I said before, the last by-elections, and particularly that of West Peterborough, are an indication of the popular will. I am convinced that they reflect the sentiment of the whole electorate of Canada. The question was clearly put by all the candidates, and the answer was a signal one-the majority of the Opposition candidates was overwhelming.
For my part, I do not believe that the Prime Minister could have the respect, much less the confidence, of the Canadian electors. It is he who has shaped, who * has conceived all the iniquitous laws from which we have suffered during the war. And he himself dared to boast of it in Sherbrooke, when he asserted that he was the father of conscription, and that if the thing was to be done over he was ready to repeat his measure.
The hon. Prime Minister is the man who in all circumstances was the instrument of the Government. He it was who devised the closure, the muzzling of the members of the Opposition and of all those who were here to defend the interests of the people. He was also, probably, the one who contrived the censure of the press in order to prevent the electors of Canada from being

to the misappropriation or the maladministration of public funds.
A third reason which has suggested itself to my mind as a good and sufficient one why, if sustained, I could vote against the Government, is this-the enunciation of such a policy as, in the judgment of the members of Parliament, is detrimental to the prosperity and welfare of the country. If this Government were to enunciate and set forth such a policy as, in my humble opinion, would be detrimental to the prosperity and welfare of the Dominion of Canada, I should feel bound to support the present amendment. But what are the facts of the case? They are that the policy, so far as it has been enunciated in the spoken word and the published statements of the first minister of the Crown, is such as commends itself most heartily to my mind and judgment. I believe that policy, as clearly as I can understand his words, is in the highest interest of the country from a commercial, social and national standpoint. Why then should I vote against such a policy? I endorse the spirit and also the substance of his published language and of his spoken word, because those words have been uniform. I have heard him in the province by the Pacific; I have heard him in this city; I have read what he has said on the prairies; I have read what he has said east of the Ottawa river, and in every place and in every province he has told the same story.
There has been the enunciation of the same fiscal policy, namely, proper protection for all Canadian industries. I would that I could emphasize that little word " all," because, Sir, it includes the labour of the entire Canadian population. The policy looks towards the protection, not of any one class, or of any one people, or of any one section of the community, but it is a policy which aims to foster and promote the highest development and prosperity of all our Canadian industries, and our Canadian industries are manifold. They are not restricted to the manufacturers; they are not restricted to the cities; they cover the country from ocean to ocean, and, Sir, a fiscal policy that seeks to protect and preserve and encourage all legitimate Canadian industries is a policy such as I feel disposed to endorse and support.
There is another thought in the published statements and spoken words of the Prime Minister which appeals to me very strongly. I know that it has not been very seriously emphasized in this debate, but I see in it possibilities of great things in the

future. I refer to what I believe to be his honest and sincere and genuine purpose and intention to do all within his power as First Minister of the Crown to unify the Canadian people. Sir, this is no time, even by insinuation, and much less by ridicule, to throw any slur or cast any reflection upon such a high and noble purpose. It may be said by some that unification is impossible. I grant that in some respects that is true, but in other respects unification is not only possible, but in the interest of Canada it is absolutely necessary. True it is, that from ocean to ocean there are varied interests, and in some respects we cannot all be united. We may never be united in our religious convictions. There is no desire on the part of any one, I hope, to have a recognized state religion in this country. We do not wish that; the country repudiates the thought. The desire of the people of Canada is that every man shall have the right of private opinion and action with regard to his own religious views and further that there should be no official recognition by the State of any particular body, class or creed but that all should stand on a common footing before the law of the land. There canont be unity so far as a great national religion is concerned. Nobody wants it, nobody expects it.
Neither can we be united politically; I suppose that goes without saying. But there is a sense in which I believe the Prime Minister is looking towards unity on a higher, or national plane; that is to say, we can be divided in opinions, but united in aim. This may be old and oft-trodden ground, but, Sir, we cannot traverse it too often. There is in our country room for division of opinion on great national questions, on great political principles, and so long as the division is along the line of principles I have absolutely nothing to say against it. I welcome it. I believe it is a healthful sign of public thought and public sentiment. What I deplore is the existence in this great country of anything which would even appear to divide province against province, or class against class, or one section of the country against another section. We may be divided on great national issues; we should on these be divided; but in the name of our common country let us divide on lines of principle or policy and not on lines of class, not on lines of religion, not on lines of race, not even on lines of language. We cannot afford it. Our country is too big

and potential, the future of this Dominion is too vast in its importance to allow anything of that character to interfere with or retard our true national prosperity.
There has been, in late years, arising a class consciousness as we are all aware. There is room for a class consciousness, and there will issue from it certain results to the advantages of the class, its progress and development, locally, and socially, but when we step into the larger realm of national affairs and national policies, I claim, Sir, that we should be first, last, and always, Canadian citizens. I sit in this Chamber by the grace of the votes of my people, a fruit grower, here to my right is a lawyer, to my left a manufacturer, behind me are two doctors, across the aisle is a grain-grower from Saskatchewan, and another from Manitoba; but we are not here as lawyers, or grain-growers, or doctors, or manufacturers: we are here as Canadian citizens.
During the last few months we have had two by-elections in the province from which I come. Considerable has been said in this House about by-elections, and I want to tell you something about these two byelections in my province. One was in the city of Victoria, the other in the constituency of Yale and, Sir, it is a matter of history, a matter of fact, that in neither of these cases was there an Opposition candidate in the field representing the official Opposition in this House. In the city of Victoria there was a combination of opponents of the Government, but without an issue, without the semblance of a platform-they were simply against the Government. What did we find in Yale, where the second by-election took place? We had the Government candidate standing on the Government record and on the Government policy. Did my Liberal friends put a candidate in the field in Yale? No, they did not, although at one time, I am told, they intended to. What was done? It was decided by the Liberals of Yale in written resolution that in view of the situation which obtained, all the opponents of the Government candidate, should unite in order to "defeat the common enemy" and therefore they endorsed the Opposition candidate.	_
That was the situation in Yale-no policy, no principle, simply a combination of some Liberals, some returned soldiers, some farmers, and some extreme Labour men who united their forces in support of one man who, when he received their endorsa-tion, turned round and said: "I repudiate
the whole of you; I will be an independent." My friends the Agrarians, through their representatives, have been doing their utmost to win to their political bosom the farmers from my province. That is perfectly legitimate. I presume that courtship is always in order. Up to the present the farmers in my constituency-and I have the honour to represent one of the finest rural constituencies in the Dominion of Canada-and the farmers of my province as a whole have not responded to their solicitations. They have stretched out their hands across the Rockies and with a firm grasp have said: "We are brithers a', but first and last we are Canadian citizens and we shall not enter into any political alliance with the agrarian movement of the Prairies."
Now, I stand here to-night as a farmer, but not as a class man. I believe that it is the right and the privilege of the members of any class to unite for the advancement of their own local interests, of their own business or profession; but in the higher sphere of national deliberation, let us meet as Canadian citizens
9 p.m. to promote the interests of all classes and conditions of people in the country and of the nation as a whole, irrespective of the occupations which we as members may individually pursue. I have examined as closely as I can the three main reasons which could possibly be adduced why a man should vote against the Government of the day and in favour of the amendment as proposed by the leader of the Opposition, and by way of brief review in reply let me say that this Government has kept its pre-election pledges. It has prosecuted the war to the utmost of its ability, and history will determine, as we cannot do to-night, the measure of praise which is due to Canadian arms in the final victory that was won in 1918. Now, because this Government redeemed every one of its pledges, and is now in process of winding up the business in the closing years of its record, am I to vote want of confidence in an Administration that by redeeming those pledges has brought honour to our country and established for her no small place of influence among the nations of the world? No charge of any serious character has been made against the Government. Why then should I vote against it?
The general future policy of the .Government as enunciated by the Prime Minister in his address commends itself to the people

of the Dominion, I believe. It is useless for my friends on the other side to say that the country wants a change. There is no use in saying that: the mere assertion does not make it a fact. I know that in many districts of this Dominion the people are satisfied with the present Government, and it is a weakness on the part of the Opposition to simply ask the Government to resign, and to reinforce that request by calling them names. That is only the method of school-boys in the primary classes. To say: "You are usurpers, office seekers, etc." is the policy of children and not of statesmen. Who are the office seekers? Ask that question in my district and people will smile, as well they might. When the First Minister of the Crown paid a visit to the province of British Columbia he left an impression of candour, of sincerity, of ability, and of personal power and magnetism that even his enemies admitted. More than one said to me in private: "I do not see how I can vote against a man: of that calibre;" and so to-night, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say in answer to my hon. friend from Brome that I cannot accept his invitation. I shall vote against the amendment and in favour of the motion.
Mr. 0. TURGEON (Gloucester) :	Mr. Speaker, before dealing with the subjects contained in the Address, I desire to pay my tribute of congratulation to the mover and seconder, both of whom discharged their duty in this respect in an admirable manner. While I do not endorse some of the sentiments expressed in the speeches of those gentlemen, I must say that my hon. friend who moved the Address has undoubtedly displayed on this occasion literary attainments which are not frequently met with in our day and that in his short address he has expressed noble thoughts in noble language which I am sure we all appreciate. All together he has given unmistakable evidence of the fact that the "Garden of the Gulf" can produce the best elements of humanity as well as of nutriment. My hon. friend from Yale (Mr. MacKelvie) who has made his debut is also well equipped as a parliamentarian; he shows great command of language and much depth of thought, and the House may well regard him as a valuable acquisition. Naturally the hon. member for Yale is interested in apples and wants this commodity protected. Were I in his place I would endeavour to have this choice fruit enjoyed not only in the neighbourhood of its culture, but would have it sent across

the boundary to the South so that it might tempt the American as well as the Canadian epicures. There are thousands of Canadians who would certainly greatly appreciate the extension of the field of fruit production and such an extension would be in the best interests not only of British Columbia but of the Dominion as a whole.
We now have a Prime Minister administering the destinies of the Dominion. Were the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen) present in this Chamber I think he would permit me to state that from the first day he made his appearance among us I have acknowledged his talent, his ability, his legal acumen, his subtlety and ingenuity, and, recalling the first of his speeches in Parliament, there has come to my mind this evening an incident in which there figured an old deskmate of mine, who departed this world only a few months ago, and myself. The gentleman in question enjoyed the admiration and the love of the House during the years he sat beside me- I refer to the late Mr. Leblanc, who for years sat beside me in this Parliament and who made way for the present member for Kent, N.B. (Mr. Leger). We had both carefully watched the young man who was to become the future Premier of Canada, and whose health seemed to be so frail. My deskmate of that time, who could not always follow closely the utterances of members, was accustomed to ask me what they had said and what my opinion was of their speeches. One day he inquired of me "What do you think of that young gentleman?" meaning the present Premier. I replied, "If he lives, he will rise."
My prediction has been fulfilled. The young member of that day has lived and has risen to a most commanding position, and he will undoubtedly bring to the administration of public affairs in Canada that talent and that ingenuity for which he was conspicuous when he first entered Parliament. Despite his mental equipment it seemed to be the fate of this young man to be plunged into difficulties, and in the exercise of his high duties he has undoubtedly at times been placed in a position before the country and before the Empire which perhaps he has not always enjoyed. His generosity has induced him to do his utmost to preserve his party from the fate which threatened it, and perhaps it is not too much to say that but for his ability it would have gone under before the year 1917 was reached.

In spite of my opinion of his talents I am bound to say that the present learned and capable Prime Minister has done things which have aroused suspicion in the minds of the people. Many of the doings of Parliament during the last ten years, it must be admitted, do not commend themselves to the calm judgment of the electors of Canada, including old time Conservatives as well as old time Liberals. It seems to me that his party have profited by his devotion and his talents to-I will not say ruin-but to lessen his reputation, for he was called to a better destiny than has been permitted to him as the result of his*choice of followers and friends.
May I recall one of the first pieces of legislation with which he was identified and which had an important effect upon the procedure of Parliament? I remember well the manner in which it was introduced and how it blocked our late lamented leader, who was so greatly beloved not only by Canadians but by the world at large. As a result of the change in the rules of the House, the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier on rising to speak on an amendment was obliged to sit down and to suffer in silence. He was debarred from speaking, although he had a perfect right to. When a vote was reached, I remember as well as though it were only yesterday the desertion of some seventeen or eighteen French-Can-adian members elected as Nationalists. There was one exception, the then member for Bellechasse. With him blood was thicker than water, if I may use the phrase, and he voted on the side of the Liberal leader. But each of the other members to whom I allude rose to plant a dagger in the heart of the great Liberal. The time came when every one of them disappeared from political life, with the exception of one who managed to save himself when his political ship was foundering.
Other acts of the present Prime Minister when he was Solicitor General or Minister of the Interior have not commended themselves to public approval. His coming to the front, as he has done, denotes that his talents were far above those of the rest of his colleagues in Parliament. Let me say in this connection that we have not forgotten our former great leader. As the member for St. Hyacinthe-Rouville said yesterday our former great leader is dead. True he is dead but his spirit survives and will live for centuries to come.
Yes, for a long time to come.

What are the circumstances to-day? I may be permitted to recall the conditions and the principles upon which Union Government was made possible in 1917. As a close personal friend and an enthusiastic admirer of the Hon. Prank B. Carvell, who became Minister of Public Works at the formation of Union Government, I had particular occasion to remember the conditions on which he became a member of that Government. The primary condition was that the Government of that day was formed for the period of the war and until demobilization, and no longer. My hon. friend the member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) yesterday with his usual eloquence recited to this House the explanation given at the time by the then Minister of Public Works respecting the formation of the Union Government, and that he would retire when he thought his mission was over. I wish to emphasize his election addresses at the beginning of the campaign of 1917, when he stated to the country the conditions upon which he and his colleagues entered that Government; and it must be remembered that he was telling the people those conditions before they voted, that the Government candidates were to be elected only for the duration of the war and demobilization, and no longer.
I see my sincere friend the Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Calder) looking in my direction, and I am sure that his expressions at that time were similar to those voiced by the then Minister of Public Works. They told the country that they and their colleagues were joining the Union Government for one purpose only, for the carrying on of the war, and when that had been brought to a successful conclusion they would return to their party. They did not say that they were joining the Government for a term of five years; no, they were educating the electorate to the fact that as soon as the war was over they would all return to their own fold and leave the Conservative party to its own fate.
Let me quote from a speech delivered at Sarnia, Ontario, by the then Minister of Public Works, Mr. Carvell, at a convention for the selection of a Union Government candidate. I take this report from the St. John Telegraph, a publication which was most devoted to the minister during that campaign, so that the correctness of the

report cannot be doubted. Among other things the report says:
Mr. Carvell told of the great efforts made to prevent a rupture in the Liberal ranks,

but it failed.
"But* we men who disagreed with Sir Wilfrid are Liberals yet, and when the war is over, we will start again where we were last week."
Mr. Carvell declared that the Liberals in the Government would not remain unless profiteering was stopped1, and unless certain things happened which he thought ought to happen.
He was telling the members of the old Government that they had been helping profiteering, and the members of that Government assented to his profession wlfen they accepted him and kept him in the Ministry. He said that that profiteering would have to stop. Quoting Mr. Carvell, the report goes on to say:
"When things don't suit us, there is no reason why we should remain. I am going through this campaign as a Liberal, as a man who has joined with his opponents for a definite time and for a definite purpose. I would a thousand1 times rather have gone to the country with my own party, but it was not to be."
It was stated, therefore, to the electors of Canada in November, 1917, that this union was formed for war purposes and that after the war was over the Liberals who had joined the Government would return to their party.
My right hon. friend claims that he is in the same position as other Prime Ministers who were called to office during a term of Parliament. Reference has been made to Sir John A. Macdonald and even to the successor of Sir Lomer Gouin in the province of Quebec. But in these cases the Parliaments had but recently been elected; the Governments in question had the confidence of the people; nothing had happened to bring about changed conditions in the ranks of the Government party or in the public mind. The conditions were not similar to those in the present case; therefore the comparison cannot fairly be made.
Well, the war being over, demobilization being completed, and a number of Government members having withdrawn their support from the Ministry, a caucus was called of the remainder of the supporters of the Government for the selection of a leader in the place of the then Prime Minister, who was retiring. The selection of the present Prime Minister may have been a wise one, but that does not alter the fact that the right hon. gentleman holds office unconstitutionally. He has

been elected not by the voice of the people, but by a remnant of supporters of the Union-a union which still remains to-day, though it has no further assistance or support from those who maintain true Liberal principles. His position, therefore, is entirely contrary to the spirit of the constitution.
Had the Prime Minister appealed to the people when he was selected for the office which he now occupies, he would have been defeated, but he would have come back with a stronger following than he will have when he does appeal to the people.
1 wish to tell him as a personal friend that the longer he delays his appeal to the people the smaller will be his guard when he comes back to this Parliament as leader of the Opposition. Possibly he would be more comfortable as leader of the Opposition than he now is as leader of the Government. I do not say that the people of Canada would be very badly off in having my hon. friend as leader of the Opposition; I would tell my Liberal colleagues that they would have to be careful in their administration so that they should not give him the chance to attack them with all the arms which he has at his disposal.
The people to-day are clamouring for an election. The returned soldiers in every province are clamouring for an election. We say that we have done a great deal for our soldiers, but we can never compensate them for the immense sacrifices which they have made. From the very beginning of the war I took a consistent attitude among the people of my constituency. I travelled over every part of my county and talked to boys, not merely to those on the street corners, but to those whose fathers and mothers had been friends of mine and who had by them been entrusted to my care and counsel. Many have come to my private office seeking aid and encouragement, which were freely given. Before conscription came into effect, 1,350 young men had left my constituency, impelled by the spirit of sacrifice, to serve their country, and of that number of young men who one after another responded to my call, 1,150 were French-Acadians. To-day those men who have returned want an election. They do not all approve of the way in which they have been treated. We told them that if they would go to the war Canada would be theirs when they came back, but on their return they have not been treated as they deserve. Every man in every walk of life in Canada to-day wants an election;

they want an expression of their will according to the Canadian constitution, the Canadian and Britfsh spirit.
I shall not enter into a discussion of the tariff. My views on this are well known, and I may have something to say when the Budget is brought before Parliament; but I should like to mention one statement made by the leader of the Government which is not justified by the situation in the country. He repated in his speech the other day that the Government of the day had reduced the tariff by a .considerable amount since the conclusion of the war and had again reduced it last year. That reduction consisted in the removal of the extra duty of 5 per cent on British imports and 71 per cent on other imports which was introduced by the Conservative Government at the beginning of the war; it was added on to the tariff which the Liberals had left to their successors in office. It was added as a war measure and, ini my estimation at the time and in my estimation still, it was a pure war measure, and when they say they have reduced the tariff by so much since the conclusion of the war, the fact is that they have only eliminated by degrees, in two sessions, that extra tariff duty of 5 and 7i per cent which was imposed as a war measure. It was, therefore, right that they should expunge it from the tariff of Canada, and for their action in doing so they deserve no eulogy, and, indeed, no consideration.
There are others who claim that the Government of the day has not given the people of Canada justice. We know what has happened since last session as regards the increase of rates on the railways. My position is not new; I did not remain silenfi until a clamour arose from the Atlantic to the Pacific against that increase of 40 per cent in rates on Canadian railways granted for the benefit of the b9ard of administration of the National Railways, the experts of Mackenzie and Mann; at the last session on more than one occasion I protested in this House to the Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) against the idea of an increase in freight rates at this time, until conditions became more settled, until we saw what the board of administration of the National Railways of Canada would be able to do.
